title: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia amid questions about her legal credentials
description: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.President Donald Trump describe
body: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week. She has referred to herself as a lawyer. But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China." She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.It is seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US. The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself. She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.The new press secretary also told the paper that when she answered China to a question about her bar exam, it was a misunderstanding. She had mistakenly thought, above the din of Marine One, the reporter had asked: "Where were you after law school?"Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment, as well as Zhong Lun Law Firm.It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work. Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

schema.headline: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia amid questions about her legal credentials

title: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
description: Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.The Ukrainian
body: Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times.Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said a slowdown of Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military was deliberate.He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.But Zelensky accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal.Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet uplinks are used throughout its war effort.There were suggestions that the slowdown to Starlink services was due to a technical fault - something owner Elon Musk appeared to deny was the case, suggesting it was the Trump administration. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing."It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT while in London.He said he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin.He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week. "We didn't destroy any relationship."Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."

schema.headline: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says

title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
description: Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast und
body: Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language. In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total. Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites". Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples." Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all". "I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting". The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

schema.headline: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments

title: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
description: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air f
body: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.US President Donald Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and  Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?

title: UK economy sees surprise growth in August ahead of Healey's first Budget
description: The UK's economy recorded surprise growth in August despite the impact of rising energy prices and borrowing costs. Official figures showed the econom
body: The UK's economy recorded surprise growth in August despite the impact of rising energy prices and borrowing costs. Official figures showed the economy expanded by 0.1% in the month, defying analysts' expectations of a slight contraction.It means the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August, and follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF).Chancellor John Healey, who will deliver his first Budget in two weeks, said the UK has shown resilience in the face of conflicts in Europe and the Middle East.Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought". He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance. "The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added. The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks."This week the IMF have upgraded UK growth for 2026 and said that our fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest deficit in the G7 forecast by 2029."He promised to build on the UK's debt reduction plans, which were praised by the IMF, and use the Budget to "provide some breathing space for today, and offer fresh hope for the future".The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.

schema.headline: UK economy sees surprise growth in August ahead of Healey's first Budget

title: Warning to women amid shortages of some HRT products
description: Dr Ursula Mason, chair of the Royal College of General Practitioners Northern Ireland, said finding a substitute "can cause real anxiety for patients"
body: Dr Ursula Mason, chair of the Royal College of General Practitioners Northern Ireland, said finding a substitute "can cause real anxiety for patients". "This can be particularly so for HRT medication when a woman has found a preparation that works well for them," she said."Patients can be assured that the protocol in place only allows a substitution for exactly the same active ingredient at the same dose. "If a woman finds that for whatever reason the new formulation is not managing their symptoms or they are having side effects, it would be important that they contact their GP to discuss both their symptoms and the options available around suitable alternatives."The Department of Health said it was aware of "supply disruptions" affecting some HRT medications across the UK, including ongoing issues with Estradot transdermal patches and a more recent disruption affecting FemSeven Conti patches. "Communications have been issued to healthcare professionals regarding the products affected, including advice on suitable alternatives that remain available," it said.It added: "Serious Shortage Protocol (SSPs) for Estradot transdermal patches are currently in place until 8 January 2027, permitting pharmacists to supply alternative products to patients without the need for a new prescription, where the patient has agreed to this."If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to a healthcare professional for advice about their treatment options."Roisin Hillman, co-founder of Menopause Together, Northern Ireland's first menopause support charity, noted some women forced to switch brands due to medication shortages have reported side effects like itchy skin or patches falling off.She said that ongoing HRT patch shortages are deeply frustrating for women. Once they find a medication that works, it often falls in short supply."This is an issue going on for years," she said advising women to request longer-term prescriptions from their GPs to stay ahead of supply gaps.She also warned against sharing HRT with others."It is also really important that if you do have a shortage, and you can't get your normal HRT, to make sure you go back to your doctor."Please do not share HRT with other women because what is prescribed to you may not suit someone else so it is very important that you go back to your GP," she said."I know that when women have that fear and anxiety that the HRT they are on is helping so many aspects of their life and in particular a woman's mental health."If she on HRT that works for her and then if she is not getting that HRT it can be really hard."

schema.headline: Warning to women amid shortages of some HRT products

title: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms
description: A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings wit
body: A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country."This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast," the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it. "I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC. A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernautA new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators. Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.  There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand. "This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US senator working on data centre legislation."There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the pushback against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago."People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran war and various aspects of the economy.Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.Yet, recent research, external from the Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centre project.Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees. Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials. Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres."This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle," the NRSC added.  Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed. Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".It could play a part in the state's upcoming Senate race too.Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand."There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project. "She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

schema.headline: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms

title: Formula 1: The pit stop that helped save lives
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A seven-second McLaren pit stop inspired a new approach to patient care that saved livesByEllie ManF1 journal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A seven-second McLaren pit stop inspired a new approach to patient care that saved livesByEllie ManF1 journalistWhen the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.Image source, Great Ormond Street Hospital/University of OxfordImage caption, How hospitals used inspiration from F1 for surgery-to-ICU handovers Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step."And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up."It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.From trackside to bedsideFifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.Image source, University Hospital of WalesImage caption, Gemma Fisher (left) and doctors from the University Hospital of WalesStandardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.Every second countsF1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

schema.headline: Formula 1: The pit stop that helped save lives

title: Fifa: Could Arsene Wenger take on Gianni Infantino for presidency?
description: Despite the backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors, Fifa president Gianni Infantino looks
body: Despite the backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors, Fifa president Gianni Infantino looks increasingly likely to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next year.But could there be a sensational twist?Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate.But would the man who has been the governing body's head of global development since 2019 really challenge his own boss? And what lies behind the support he has?On Thursday the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since the emergence of Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme plunged the organisation into crisis, leading to calls from the game's leaders in Europe, North America and Asia for him to step down.A defiant Infantino will come face to face with some of his fiercest critics at what could be a spicy gathering in Zurich.Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development. But Infantino will also face scrutiny over governance reforms, FFE, the awarding of the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize last year to US President Donald Trump, and disciplinary procedures in the wake of the Folarin Balogun affair.But the meeting will also bring into sharp focus the failure so far to identify a unifying figure with the worldwide appeal to challenge Infantino.While potential rivals like Victor Montagliani, the president of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (Concacaf), and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders, Infantino has been busy touring the world, shoring up his position.The growing expectation is that such is the support he retains in his power base of Africa, South America and Oceania, he will be returned, despite only carrying the backing of roughly half of Fifa's 211 members.To date, the only person to declare their intention to run is the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although few rate his chances.So could Wenger be the answer?Here in Zurich, there is no indication that he is plotting a bid. On Wednesday evening Wenger joined Infantino and other Fifa Council members for dinner in a Zurich restaurant. As a senior member of Fifa's management team, he will also be present at Thursday's meeting.When BBC Sport asked about his intentions via Fifa, no comment was provided. Meanwhile, those close to the 76 year-old, who left Arsenal in 2018 after 22 years in which he became the most successful manager in the club's history, will not be drawn on whether he is interested.One told BBC Sport he would be "an ideal candidate, but he is his own man". A high-ranking Fifa official insisted he had no idea if Wenger was tempted.But what is clear is that he does have supporters, who believe he commands the level of respect beyond Europe that would be essential if the Uefa-led rebellion against Infantino is to have any chance of success."He's a brilliant football man who truly understands football development because he's been running it," claimed one senior official at a European national association."People don't see him as just a European. He's very respected in Asia, for instance, from his time working in Japan. A lot of people are saying he'd be the ideal candidate. With him, it's not about money, status or ego. He genuinely loves the game."He's made a difficult role work and understands Fifa, and that's why he'd be a really good candidate."That said, he's in a really difficult position."That was highlighted amid the fallout over FFE, when Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot."I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said in a statement at the time. "The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."Some may have expected Wenger to resign over the controversy, given his thinly veiled criticism of Infantino, the way he had been kept in the dark, and the condemnation of the plot from stakeholders across the game. But he has carried on in a role in which he oversees youth development at academies in 60 countries, as well as youth competitions around the world. He is also a technical adviser to rule-making body International Football Association Board (Ifab).Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups, and the idea of a 'daylight' offside law.But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.Indeed, at the weekend Wenger was in Cape Verde at a Confederation of African Football conference, telling the delegates: "We want to see an African team win the World Cup, and the numbers show that it is feasible."Such sentiments would do him no harm if he was to stand for president.BBC Sport has been told that a large number of Fifa's staff also want Wenger to run, and believe he could change the organisation's image.Others, however, are more sceptical. One well-connected figure in Fifa circles told BBC Sport that he would be "amazed if Wenger would rise up against the man who appointed him in the first place. Arsene has had some fairly 'out there' ideas. In terms of the administration of the game and the relationships on a political level, in the kind of places you're going to need to corral and command power, I'm not sure he's the man for that."Another senior European official said: "He has the stature, but I'm not sure he smacks of the future. Maybe he could do a single term to introduce reforms. He is very respected in the game and has done a good job of the development programmes, but whether he'd split from Gianni, I just don't know."If Wenger does want to run, he has until 18 November to declare his candidacy, and would need to be nominated by at least five national associations.As a manager, Wenger is remembered as a legendary figure who changed English football with his forward-thinking approach to tactics and nutrition.Could he attempt a shake-up of a different kind at Fifa? It is an intriguing prospect.

schema.headline: Fifa: Could Arsene Wenger take on Gianni Infantino for presidency?

title: Bradley Barcola arrives in style as Liverpool beat LASK in Champions League
description: On the eve of Liverpool's meeting with LASK, manager Andoni Iraola was repeatedly asked about the fortunes of Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.Given
body: On the eve of Liverpool's meeting with LASK, manager Andoni Iraola was repeatedly asked about the fortunes of Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.Given their price tags, the pressure was on both to start delivering after stuttering starts to their individual campaigns. Iraola, as most managers would, stood by his players, insisting he trusted them "100%". Iraola insisted the focus was on the collective rather than individual stats but there is no denying that when you spend such eye-watering sums - £116m on Wirtz and £123m on Barcola - you want those players to be match-winners.Wirtz delivered a fine display in the Austrian city of Linz as Liverpool won 6-3, with an assist to show for his efforts. However, this was a night where the headlines belonged to Barcola, who on the 238th appearance of his career across clubs and country combined, scored his first hat-trick.And it was those three goals which proved to be the difference as Liverpool returned to winning ways after their 3-0 loss to Manchester City on Sunday. In truth, the 24-year-old could have scored more such was his quality, but he did enough to take the match ball home after two fine finishes with his right foot and left foot, followed by a tap in after the break.And a little over 24 hours after defending his players against  those pre-match questions, Iraola was speaking with a smile on his face. "I'm really happy for Bradley," Iraola said."You were asking me yesterday about him not making the numbers and [the same with] Florian and I think both of them today played really, really well. I think they made a difference."Bradley was a threat, always when one-on-one [and] certainly in behind. He helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them."I think for their confidence it's very good.  I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. I think it's going to be very good, very good for them."On what it could mean for Barcola, Iraola added: "I think he has to enjoy this [as] to score a hat-trick in the Champions League is always very difficult. "Even yesterday in training, I could feel he was very lively. Sometimes you feel these things [are going to happen]. We were feeling he was in a good place going into the game."Barcola will now hope to show that level in the Premier League, starting with a visit to Brentford on Saturday.Iraola's side were relentless in the first-half against the Austrian Bundesliga champions, racing into a three-goal lead. Such was their dominance, they could have easily scored more.The 19 shots Liverpool had by half time against LASK was the most on record since 2003-04 by any team in the first half of a Champions League away match. If there was any criticism, it would be that they were guilty of becoming a little complacent in the second half, conceding three goals after the hour mark but in fairness, the job was all but done.There were more positives to take on the night, with both full-backs coming into the side and performing well. Jeremie Frimpong scored and registered two assists while Kostas Tsimikas added two assists of his own. Ronald Araujo also scored his first goal for the club since joining in the summer and Lewis Koumas got no less than he deserved when he got on the scoresheet in the second half. The 21-year-old even had two goals ruled out for offside but his first-half assist for Barcola meant that he became the youngster player to score and assist in a  Champions League match for Liverpool (21y 25d), with the previous youngest being Steven Gerrard (21y 139d v Dynamo Kyiv in 2001). Fine company, indeed.But Liverpool will know that they won’t get many easier games than this over the course of the season. LASK came into this game, winless in their past four matches.“What do you take from that? It's very difficult because the game was very passive for large periods,” said Stephen Warnock on 5 Live.”There were parts where I am watching Trey Nyoni in midfield and he has literally got no pressure on him at all, he is picking passes off.“Barcola has got the run of his full-back who was taken off at half-time, which tells you everything.“I don't read too much into it, because I expected Liverpool to go there and win, and win comfortably."Warnock added that a bigger test for Liverpool will come at Brentford on Saturday, the Bees fourth in the table and unbeaten in the league.“Can Barcola do that again, away at Brentford, because that is what they have essentially bought him for, to play in big games away from home," Warnock said.“He hasn't played that much football this season so [this game] was about getting minutes in his legs and getting him fit and getting him sharper. The acid test will be Brentford away.”

schema.headline: Bradley Barcola arrives in style as Liverpool beat LASK in Champions League

title: Fall in West Midlands gun crime down to policing and community efforts
description: More than 10 years ago, the West Midlands was dubbed the gun crime capital of England and Wales. It was an area suffering from high-profile shootings.
body: More than 10 years ago, the West Midlands was dubbed the gun crime capital of England and Wales. It was an area suffering from high-profile shootings. Gun fights between rival gangs were happening regularly.Figures at the time reflected that notoriety - there were more firearms offences per head in the West Midlands Police force area than anywhere else."Back then, there were shootings every day, reported shootings every day and unreported shootings every day," says Simeon Moore, also known as Zimbo, an ex-Johnson crew member - one of the Birmingham's most notorious gangs in the noughties.New figures seen by BBC News show shootings in the West Midlands force area - covering Birmingham, Wolverhampton, the Black Country and Coventry - have dropped significantly over the past six years."Things have calmed down dramatically since the early 2000s," Zimbo, who now mentors youngsters, said.While the numbers are not directly comparable, due to the criteria in the way they were gathered and published, in 2002-03 the force recorded about 1,300 gun crimes, external, compared with 504 in the 2024 calendar year, external.A more direct snapshot of the past six years also shows things are improving.In 2020-21, there were  a total of 157 firearms discharges, while a year later in 2021-2022 there were 148.By last year, the number of discharges had dropped to 69 and in the first seven months of 2026, there had only been 30, according to figures from West Midlands Police.The force said the fall was down to way it now dealt with firearms incidents. A major crime unit deals with all firearms events. Every time gun fire is reported, it is treated as if it was a murder.But it is not all down to policing, Zimbo said.He thinks there has been a change in culture, with more people speaking out about that kind of lifestyle, keeping the next generation out of trouble.He was jailed for six years for possessing a semi-automatic weapon as a teenager and was in and out of prison for two decades."We lived it," Zimbo said."There's more people that have been involved in that life talking about it, turning away from it and speaking bad about it in the sense that this isn't the right way to go."Now you've got man that have lived that life, done crazy sentences and they're telling the young people now, 'if you're going to start living like this, expect jail, expect to lose your friends or possibly lose your own life.'"At Revere Records in the city, where Zimbo heads up its urban division, a young artist, Solitary, is recording a track. His lyrics reference life in parts of the city, avoiding jail and being a product of your environment.This is just one of the projects Zimbo is involved with that gives youngsters opportunities. Zimbo added: "It's very hard for these young people to stay away from the lifestyle."West Midlands Police believes the reorganisation and creation of its major crime unit has led to the fall in gun crime, and a rise in seizures of weapons.Det Supt Ryan Chambers said the unit specialised in the most serious elements of criminality, targeting offenders and those in possession of firearms.He said 50% of the discharges the force dealt with were from shotguns which had been owned lawfully, but stolen in burglaries and ended up in criminal hands.Chambers said: "We've had a good level of success over the last 12-months. We've had the most recoveries and biggest reduction in discharges we've seen in recent years."

schema.headline: Fall in West Midlands gun crime down to policing and community efforts

title: Manchester City 2-4 PSG: Pep Guardiola returns but European champions humble City
description: Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaosFigure caption, Highlights: Impressive PSG beat Manchester City 4-2 at the Etiha
body: Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaosFigure caption, Highlights: Impressive PSG beat Manchester City 4-2 at the EtihadByChief football writer at Etihad StadiumManchester City returned to the welcoming surroundings of home for the first time since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations awash with defiance and presenting an 'us against the world' united front.Pep Guardiola was back at the place he decorated with success for a decade in a public show of support to embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and chief executive Ferran Soriano, the Catalan a low-key presence clad in a flat cap sitting a row behind the pair.If his appearance was relatively under the radar, the fact that he chose a game certain to attract a global audience to make his return was heavy with significance.Guardiola is ignoring the outside noise to back his former bosses to clear their name on appeal after the guilty verdict passed down by an independent commission.The stand bearing his name was emblazoned with a 'CTID' - City 'Til I Die - mosaic, while the build-up to kick-off saw a display of fireworks and pyrotechnics worthy of several rock concerts.The strategy to show an unabashed City ready to face down any enemy was going well, until the game kicked off and Champions League holders Paris St-Germain produced a ruthless first-half reality check cloaked within the brutal beauty of their football.With City providing a dramatic backdrop off the pitch, the game more than matched the setting. A second-half revival ensured embarrassment was avoided - and instead gave us a classic as PSG eventually prevailed 4-2.Figure caption, PSG run riot against Man CityCity's first step back into the limelight on the hostile territory of Anfield on Sunday ended with a 3-0 win at Liverpool and wild celebrations.Here, with Guardiola watching on from the directors' box with an agonised expression mirroring that of successor Enzo Maresca in his technical area, City ran headlong into a whirlwind of magnificent football from Luis Enrique's PSG, the half-time scoreline of 3-0 actually doing them a kindness.To City's great credit, and also Maresca's after he made three half-time changes, they responded superbly after the break, creating a host of chances.It did not retrieve what was lost in the first half, but it did at least allow City's fans to ramp up a frenzied atmosphere and give their team a rousing send-off at the final whistle.In these surroundings, there was no question of any backlash against City's Abu Dhabi-based owners, despite the fact they were found guilty of such serious financial charges to leave the club in crisis and attracting pariah status.The damage was done in PSG's staggering opening 45 minutes, with Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha the scorers as City were ripped apart.A game that began in a wall of sound, with Guardiola's name resounding around the stadium at kick-off, was reduced to stunned silence in the first 15 minutes.City, so composed and ordered amid the toxicity of Anfield on Sunday, were shell-shocked on home territory as even born streetfighters such as Enzo Fernandez were reduced to chasing shadows.The players who rose in the face of the storm raging around Manchester City at Liverpool suddenly looked like they were carrying the weight of the world on their shoulders, which made their outstanding display after the break even more praiseworthy.Guardiola looked just as engaged as when he was managerImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pep Guardiola appeared to go through every motion during Manchester City's 4-2 defeatErling Haaland gave City hope, which looked to be snuffed out when goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, who had a very poor night against his former club, saved from Maghnes Akliouche, only to see the ball drop behind him into the net.Guardiola sometimes looked just as engaged as he did when he prowled the touchline here at Etihad Stadium, collecting the trophies now being called into question.When Josko Gvardiol had a header cleared off the line Guardiola clutched his face in anguish. When Haaland scored a goal that threatened to offer City an unlikely lifeline, he remained seated but pumped his fists into the air.If the Catalan was a neutral observer, he would have relished a game of glorious chaos, the first half embellished by PSG before City mounted superb momentum after the break.As a lover of pure football with the emphasis placed firmly on attack, he may have enjoyed it anyway. The post-match discussion with Maresca would certainly have had a busy agenda.Maresca felt he saw enough to give City hope should they meet PSG again later in the Champions League, despite the manner in which they were dismantled in the first half."I really like playing against PSG because they are brave," said Maresca. "We know the way they want to press. They go man-to-man and they are very dynamic on the ball. They are the best team in Europe. They play fantastic football."But I think we are there. The reason why we struggled was because we conceded two early goals so quickly. When you are on the pitch you might think this is difficult, but in the second half we created enough to maybe deserve something."We feel sorry for the first half but I think we're quite happy now."'Goals, goals and more goals'Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha, watching for Match of the Day, described it as "great entertainment", but "not a normal game of football"."I don't feel like both teams were going at it at the same time," he said. "In the first half, PSG were excellent and City looked really off the pace. As a consequence they were heavily punished and the game basically left them."But then in the second half they have made some changes, they have rallied, knowing they are playing in front of their own crowd and their performance had to be better. So, it was more aggressive and more on the front foot, and that's why we saw those crazy scenes where it was shot after shot by City."If these two teams had played this game in matchweek six or seven, it would not have looked like this. There would have been more defensive solidity from both sides and they would probably have approached the game in a different manner."But at this stage, as we have kind of seen with some of the other games tonight, it is just goals, goals and more goals."Either way, the superb Enrique remains the scourge of the Premier League, adding another win against City to a Champions League victims list that includes Liverpool, Aston Villa, Tottenham Hotspur and Arsenal, in a semi-final then last season's final.Enrique is currently master of all he surveys in Europe as leader of this wonderful PSG team.For Maresca and City, it is back to domestic business at home to Ipswich Town on Saturday – and all the uncertainty that brings with the Premier League in a state of limbo as they await sanctions and the result of their appeal.Follow Manchester City on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical City contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about City

schema.headline: Manchester City 2-4 PSG: Pep Guardiola returns but European champions humble City

title: Gareth Southgate: Former England boss unlikely to return to club management
description: Former England manager Gareth Southgate says he does not see himself returning to club management in the Premier League.The 56-year-old has been out o
body: Former England manager Gareth Southgate says he does not see himself returning to club management in the Premier League.The 56-year-old has been out of management since resigning as Three Lions boss after guiding them to the final of Euro 2024, where they lost to Spain.Southgate, who also took England to the Euro 2020 final, has not managed at club level since a three-year spell with Middlesbrough from 2006.When asked if he would consider a return to managing in the Premier League, he told The Amol Rajan Connection podcast: "I don't see a scenario where I do that."He added: "Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying, at the very least for a period, the wins keep you going. "By the end, I didn't even enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes. So, I've hardly watched football."I went to the FA Cup final to see my team, Crystal Palace, win their first trophy. I've not been to a football ground since. So my sort of desire to be involved in football has changed."Since leaving the England role, Southgate has also spent time working in the media and earlier this year he fronted a BBC documentary where he travelled across the UK to understand challenges facing young men and boys.He has also spent time as a visiting lecturer at Harvard Business School in Boston."I've loved the last 18 months of my life," he added. "I've had 37 years where my sense of self depended on did I win or lose on Saturday. And actually I've loved having different experiences. I've met politicians, I've met people in the media industry, I have learned about leadership in all sorts of areas, I've travelled around the world learning things. "I've just enjoyed playing a different film in my life."Last month, Manchester City were found guilty of the majority of charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".The club have denied any wrongdoing and submitted an appeal on 2 October."There'll be the tribal fans' response to punish Manchester City as much as we can, relegate them, fine them, do whatever you can," added Southgate."I've been in football boardrooms, I've been in meetings with Uefa, I've been in meetings with Fifa, I have been in all these spaces and I know how complicated all of this is."My underlying thought is none of this is good for football and there are no winners because if you're at the Premier League, for a very brief moment you might feel justified that all the flak you've had for this case taking so long, this is why it's taken so long and there's the verdict, and I'm sure there's an element of justification in that."Then there's this realisation of how do we deal with all of this because you know the possibility of all the different legal cases that emerge from this, how long this could still take, what's the right sort of punishment, how do you keep the whole game on track? "That's unbelievably complex."

schema.headline: Gareth Southgate: Former England boss unlikely to return to club management

title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
description: The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career."She said that "regardless of who the wom
body: The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career."She said that "regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred"."His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious," she told the court.The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be "nice when he wanted to be, funny - undoubtedly - charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return".But she said he would also be "demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite - childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met".The prosecutor said Brand would "appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred" after the encounters.She added that "sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened".On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences.The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told.She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her.The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident".He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity".The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her.She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm.She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in – oh go on."The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004.Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told.The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets.The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard."He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' – to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal."The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively".She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said.The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009.The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion.The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell.They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further."She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry."The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009.He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said.After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting".On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence.Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999."He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far."Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'."Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far".The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday.He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

schema.headline: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
